1.text:
The surah opens by turning to everyone at once. "O humanity! Be mindful of your Lord Who created you from a single soul" is the first phrase, and it is addressed to the whole human race rather than to one town or one community. The command is to be mindful, which means keeping a careful watch over oneself, and the Lord it names is the One Who made each person from a single origin. "and from it He created its mate" moves from that origin to the pair that came out of it, so the human race is traced back to one soul and then to two. "and through both He spread countless men and women" completes the line, since from that pair came a great number of men and women spread over the earth in many shapes and colours. The three phrases together give the reason for everything that follows in the surah, because people who share one origin owe one another what that origin implies. "And be mindful of Allah" then repeats the command in a second form, and the change matters: the first call was to the Lord who made people, and this one is a call to Allah Himself. "in Whose Name you appeal to one another" names the custom by which people ask one another for things by God, so that the name of God is part of the everyday request and not only of worship. "and honour family ties" gives the third duty, which is that the bonds of kinship are not to be cut, and the verse places them beside the fear of God so that the two are held together. "Surely Allah is ever Watchful over you" closes the verse with the reason for all three commands, which is that the One who is feared and named is also the One who keeps watch over every person and sees what they do.

**All human beings are one by birth.**

All human beings are one and the same by birth. Ultimately, everyone can trace his origin to the same man and woman as father and mother. It is, therefore, necessary that all human beings should have a feeling of affinity with each other and live with fairness and goodwill like the members of one extended family. This racial unity becomes more compact in family relationships and the importance of decent behaviour among kinsfolk becomes further heightened. Good behaviour between fellow human beings is important, not merely from the moral point of view, but rather as a matter of personal concern to man himself. (O mankind!) [he said:] 'This is an expression of general applicability, but it could also be of particular applicability.

**Created from one soul, and spread as many men and women.**

O people of Makkah fear your Lord that is His punishment by being obedient to Him Who created you of a single soul Adam and from it created its mate Eve Hawwā’ from one of his left ribs and from the pair of them Adam and Eve scattered separated and spread many men and many women; and fear God by whom you claim your rights from one another tassā’alūna the original tā’ of tatasā’alūna has been assimilated with the sīn; a variant reading has tasā’alūna so that one of you says to the other ‘I ask you by God…’ or ‘For God’s sake…’; and fear kinship ties lest you sever them a variant reading of wa’l-arhāma ‘and kinship ties’ is wa’l-arhāmi as a supplement to the pronoun contained in bihi sc. From the two of them, He spread many people, both male and female, all over the earth. (And from him He created his wife) Hawwa' , who was created from Adam's left rib, from his back while he was sleeping. (And from them both He created many men and women;) means, Allah created from Adam and Hawwa' many men and women and distributed them throughout the world in various shapes, characteristics, colors and languages. Allah mentioned that He has created mankind from a single father and a single mother, so that they feel compassion for each other and are kind to the weaker among them.

**Mindful of Allah when requesting others by Him.**

Be mindful of Allah when requesting others by Him, such as: (Be careful of your duty towards Allah) obey Allah (in Whom ye claim (your rights) of one another) your stuff and rights by Allah's right, (and towards the wombs (that bare you) and also by the right of kinship and filiation; or it could also mean: keep the ties of kinship and do not sever them. (through Whom you demand your mutual (rights), is in reference to when some people say, "I ask you by Allah, and then by the relation of the Rahim (the womb, i.e. my relationship to you)", according to Ibrahim, Mujahid and Al-Hasan. Ad-Dahhak said; "Fear Allah Whom you invoke when you conduct transactions and contracts. They used to implore one another by ties of kinship.

**The wombs and the ties of kinship.**

Also, be mindful of breaking relations with your blood ties. But, the fulfillment of the rights of those in one's own charge - children, parents, husband and wife, and orphans - and the rights of other relatives which fall on each other - all depend upon civilized behaviour, respect, loving and caring, and above all on that genuinely heartfelt desire to do what is good for them. According to a hadith, God proclaimed, ‘I shall associate Myself with one who strengthens the ties of kinship and detach Myself from one who severs them. The virtues of fair dealing and compassion are general requirements of human society, but so vital are they to maintaining good family relations that in importance they stand second only to God. " "And revere the womb by not cutting the relations of the womb, but keep and honor them, as Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Al-Hasan, Ad-Dahhak, Ar-Rabi', and others have stated. (And have Taqwa of Allah through Whom you demand your mutual (rights) and revere the wombs), protect yourself from Allah by your acts of obedience to Him. He shall ask you about that which He has commanded you of acts of obedience and keeping ties of kinship.

**Watchful over you, and the reckoning.**

(Surely, Allah is always watching over you.) means, He watches all your deeds and sees your every circumstance. This part of the Ayah encourages having a sense of certainty that Allah is always watching, in a complete and perfect manner. Surely God has been watchful over you heedful of your deeds for which He will requite you that is to say He is ever possessed of such an attribute. Allah watches over you and nothing you do escapes Him; rather, He takes it into account and repays you accordingly. (Lo! Allah hath been a Watcher over you) He has been a Protector: This is so, because everyone is governed by the Great, Almighty God, who as the Reckoner for one and all, will decide the eternal future of all human beings in the Hereafter, requiting them according to their actions in this world.

**Taqwa, the command the surah opens with.**

The present Surah begins with Taqwa in the mode of command. Hence, the Surah opens with the command of Taqwa when it says: ‌ ( O men, fear your Lord). Then, alongwith the command of 'ittaqu' (fear) the word used is 'Rabb' (Lord) which has been selected out of the most fair names of Allah. As pointed out elsewhere too, this is typical of the usual style of the Holy Qura'n when it does not introduce laws in sheer cold print like the laws of the governments of this world, but puts them forth in the manner of education, training and affection by not restricting itself to the word of law alone, but by combining it with the grooming of minds and hearts as well. "O center point of human nature, O attribute of mortal nature, make godwariness your shelter and cling to it, for the life of the servants is through it and the deliverance of the travelers in it. " Godwariness is for the servant to make the commands of the Shariah into his shield so that the arrows of prohibition may not reach him. First, he takes refuge in the sentence of tawḤīd and avoids every associationism.

2.text:
The verse is about money that belongs to someone who cannot yet look after it. "Give orphans their wealth when they reach maturity" is the command, and it sets the moment of return at adulthood, when the child is able to manage what is his. "and do not exchange your worthless possessions for their valuables" names the first wrong, which is to trade what is poor for what is good. "nor cheat them by mixing their wealth with your own" names the second, which is to merge the two accounts so that the orphan's share is lost inside the guardian's. "For this would indeed be a great sin" is the verdict, and the verse gives it in plain terms so that no guardian can treat it as a small matter. The verse follows the one before, which set out the duty to the orphan as a duty of the family, and it makes that duty concrete in money. The word for orphan here is the one used for a child who has lost his father, and the verse is about that child specifically, since his father is no longer there to guard the money. The guardian stands in the father's place, and the verse asks him to do what the father would have done, which is to hand over the whole of the property once the child is grown and to keep his own goods apart from it. The three verbs of the verse are give, do not exchange, and do not mix, and each of them names a separate way in which the guardian could take what is not his, so the verse takes the trouble to name all three.

**The orphan's wealth, and the age of maturity.**

When a child attains maturity, that is, becomes pubert, he is no more referred to as yatim in the terminology of Islamic law as it has been clarified in a hadith which says: that is, 'Orphanhood ends with puberty'. So, the statement: 'give the orphans their property', in this verse, has been clarified a little later in verse 5 where it has been said that the property of the orphans should be given to them after it is certain that they have become mature and do have the ability to distinguish between what is good for them and what is not. Now, the second verse carries the command to protect the properties of the orphans, as well as the prohibition of any misappropriation therein because the guardian of an orphaned child is usually one of his relatives. Allah commands that the property of the orphans be surrendered to them in full when they reach the age of adolescence, and He forbids using or confiscating any part of it. The following was revealed regarding an orphan who demanded his property from his guardian but was refused it Give the orphans the under-age ones that have no father their property when they have reached maturity and do not exchange the evil the unlawful for the good the lawful that is taking the one in place of the other as you do when you take what is good from the orphan’s property and leave him your faulty property instead; and absorb not their property by adding it into your property; surely that the absorbing of it is a great crime a serious sin.

**The exchange of the bad for the good.**

(and do not exchange (your) bad things for (their) good ones;) Sa'id bin Al-Musayyib and Az-Zuhri commented, "Do not substitute a weak animal of yours for a fat animal (of the orphans). " Ibrahim An-Nakha'i and Ad-Dahhak commented, "Do not give something of bad quality for something of good quality. Do not exchange what is permitted for what is prohibited: taking what is good and valuable from the property of the orphans and replacing it with something bad and of little worth from your own property. (Exchange not the good for the bad (in your management) do not consume their wealth which is prohibited for you while leaving your own wealth which is lawful for you (nor absorb their wealth into your own wealth) by mixing them. Give the orphans their property and do not exchange the evil for the good and absorb not their property into your property; surely that is a great crime:

**Mixing the orphan's property with your own.**

Also, do not take the property of the orphans and combine it with your own wealth – that is a great crime before Allah. Give the orphans their property and do not exchange the evil for the good and absorb not their property into your property; surely that is a great crime: If the protector of the orphan acts with justice and beneficence then his right is protected by God and if he behaves badly and aggressively God is his adversary. It is a major sin for a joint property to be divided in such a way that some are given valuable shares, while others are given worthless shares, only for the purpose of tallying the listed items. (and devour not their substance to your substance.) means, do not mix them together so that you eat up both, as Mujahid, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Muqatil bin Hayyan, As-Suddi and Sufyan bin Hassin stated. Therefore, spending anything from the property of the orphan unlawfully by any means whatsoever is absolutely Haram (forbidden).

**The guardian's great sin, and its weight.**

(Surely, this is a great sin.), a major and substantial sin, according to Ibn 'Abbas. (Lo! That) wrongfully consuming the wealth of the orphan (would be a great sin) which will be met by Allah's punishment. So, such guardians were forbidden to marry such orphan girls unless they treated them justly and gave them the most suitable dowry; otherwise they were ordered to marry woman besides them." 'A'ishah further said, "After that verse, the people again asked the Messenger of Allah (about marriage with orphan girls), so Allah revealed the Ayah,. The verse ends with the admonition, ‌ (It is, surely, a great sin.) Here, the word 'hub', as said by Sayyidna ibn Abbas comes from the Ethiopian language. Orphan boys and girls are the weakest members of a family or society and, therefore, dealing with them appropriately is the toughest test of one’s being imbued with the fear of God. Whoever has been given charge over others and then acts unjustly toward those under his charge his adversary is his Lord for He avenges His servants what He will not avenge for His own sake. In the terminology of Islamic law, a yatim is a child whose father has died.

**The occasion of the verse, and the man from Ghatafan who held his nephew's wealth.**

This was revealed about a man from Ghatafan who had in his possession a great amount of wealth that belonged to his orphaned nephew. When this verse was revealed he decided to separate the wealth of his nephew from his own for fear of committing a sin. This was revealed about a man from Ghatafan who had in his possession an abundant fortune which belonged to his orphaned nephew. As a result they took their dispute to the Messenger of Allah, Allah bless him and give him peace, and then this verse was revealed. When this was revealed they found it difficult to maintain guardianship over orphans and some of them had ten or eight wives under their care and did not treat them all equally and so the following was revealed. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'ishah, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Al-Hasan, Abu Malik, Abu Razin, An-Nakha'i, Ash-Sha'bi, Ad-Dahhak, 'Ata' Al-Khurasani, Qatadah, As-Suddi and Muqatil bin Hayyan that Ta'ulu means to deviate [from justice].

3.text:
The verse is about orphan girls and the marriage of women who have no one to protect them, and it is the second of the three rules that the surah builds around the orphan. "If you fear you might fail to give orphan women their due rights if you were to marry them" names the worry first, which is that a guardian who marries the girl in his care may not give her what is hers. The verse does not simply forbid such a marriage. It sets a test for it, and the test is whether the guardian can give the orphan her full due. "then marry other women of your choice, two, three, or four" is the way out the verse offers, since the guardian is free to look to other women, and the number is set as a limit as well as a permission, because the man is held to the count he chooses. The words "two, three, or four" name the range, and the range is not an invitation to take the most. "But if you are afraid you will fail to maintain justice" repeats the test in the same words, so that the rule is the same whether the wives are many or few. Justice is the thing being measured, and the verse measures it by what the man is able to keep. "then content yourselves with one or those bondwomen in your possession" gives the fallback, which is one wife, or the women who are held in the household. The choice of a single partner is the safe course for the man who fears that he cannot be fair. "This way you are less likely to commit injustice" closes the verse with the reason for the whole arrangement, which is that fewer wives make it easier to be fair to each of them, and the verse does not claim more than that. The verse follows the warning about orphans' property, and it carries that care from wealth over to marriage, so that the guardian is asked to be just with a person in the same way that he is asked to be just with a purse. The reader sees the same concern in both: the orphan must not lose by the one who keeps her.

**The orphan girl and her due rights.**

The word, 'yatama' in this verse means orphaned girls. Surely, this is a great sin And if you fear that you shall not be able to deal justly with the orphan girls, then marry (other) women of your choice, two or three, or four; but if you fear that you shall not be able to deal justly (with them), then only one or (the captives and the servants) that your right hands possess. Orphans deserve to be treated in a manner which is just and compassionate and whereby their rights are ensured the maximum protection. (And if ye fear that ye will not deal fairly by the orphans) and if you fear that you will not preserve orphans' wealth, you should also fear not dealing fairly with women in relation to providing sustenance and apportionment. This was revealed about any custodian under whose care is a female orphan who possesses some wealth and does not have anyone to defend her rights. The custodian refuses to give this orphan in marriage out of greed for her money, harms her and treats her badly. Orphan boys and girls are the weakest members of a family or society and, therefore, dealing with them appropriately is the toughest test of one’s being imbued with the fear of God.

**Why the number is four and no more.**

Allah forbade them from doing so and prohibited them from marrying more than four wives, saying: (marry of the women, who seem good to you) marry that which Allah has made lawful for you, (two or three or four) marry one, two, three or four but do not marry more than four wives; (and if ye fear that ye cannot do justice) to four wives in relation to apportionment and providing sustenance (then one (only) then marry only one free woman (or that your right hands possess) of captives, and in that case you do not owe them any apportionment, and they need not observe any waiting period. If you fear that you will not act justly toward the orphans marry such women as seem good to you two or three or four but if you fear you will not be equitable then only one or what your right hands own; thus it is likelier that you will not be unjust. You may marry two, three or four; but if you fear that you will be unjust between them, then marry just one, or suffice with what you possess of slave women, for their rights are not the same as the rights of wives. The outcome (to be seen as a whole) is that the Qur'an has permitted having four wives in marriage which means that marriages entered into within this limit will be correct and permissible.

**Justice between the wives, and the obligation.**

He mandated justice between [these wives] so the servant must respect what is obligatory. But if he knows that he will fall short in meeting this obligation he should not do it for he is accountable for what is obligatory. but if they are pleased to offer you any of it of their own accord consume it with wholesome appetite. (Thus it) marrying just one woman (is more likely that ye will not do injustice) that you will not incline to some at the expense of others or that you transgress regarding the provision of sustenance and apportionment to four wives. This is the best way to avoid being unjust or biased. Why then, it was said, by adding the word, 'adna that 'it will be closer to your not doing injustice', instead, the statement should have been something to the effect that it will make you totally safe from this injustice. The expression ma taba' in this verse, as explained by Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Jubair and Ibn Malik, may the mercy of Allah be upon them, means 'ma halla', that is, women who are lawful for you. If he knows that he can uphold this obligation in a proper manner the choice is a permitted one.

**The orphan girl the guardian withholds.**

People used to be wary of the wealth of orphans but took liberty with women and married whoever they liked. And so Allah, exalted is He, says (And if ye fear that ye will not deal fairly by the orphans marry of the women, who seem good to you) as long as they are lawful to you and leave this one . So when they asked about the orphans and the verse (Give unto orphans their wealth), regarding the orphans, was revealed, Allah, exalted is He, also revealed (And if ye fear that ye will not deal fairly by the orphans). This is the opinion of Ibn Abbas according to the narration of al-Walibi . If you fear that you will not be just in marrying the female orphans under your guardianship – fearing that you will not give them an appropriate dowry or will not treat them well – then do not marry them, and marry other women you choose. If you fear that you will not act justly that you will not be equitable towards the orphans and are thus distressed in this matter then also fear lest you be unjust towards women when you marry them; marry such mā means man women as seem good to you two or three or four that is each man may marry two or three or four but do not exceed this; but if you fear you will not be equitable towards them in terms of their expenses and individual share; then marry only one or restrict yourself to what your right hands own of slavegirls since these do not have the same rights as wives; thus by that marrying of only four or only one or resorting to slavegirls it is likelier it is nearer in outcome that you will not be unjust that you will not be inequitable.

**Women and dowries as a free gift.**

And give women their dowries as a free gift; God granted free men the right to marry four women at the same time. This was because they used to marry as many women as they liked, as many as nine or ten. Qays Ibn al-Harth for example had eight wives. In this verse, the word ('adna') has been derived from (dunuwun) which means nearness and the other word (la ta ulu) is from which means inclination or tilt. (marry of the women, who seem good to you) marry that which Allah has made lawful for you, (two or three or four) marry one, two, three or four but do not marry more than four wives; (and if ye fear that ye cannot do justice) to four wives in relation to apportionment and providing sustenance (then one (only) then marry only one free woman (or that your right hands possess) of captives, and in that case you do not owe them any apportionment, and they need not observe any waiting period.

4.text:
The verse turns from the guardian to the husband, and it is about the dowry that a man gives the woman he marries. "Give women you wed their due dowries graciously" is the command, and the word for the gift is the one that means what is owed, so the dower is not a favour but a right that falls due with the marriage. The phrase "their due dowries" makes the point that the sum is a debt the husband owes the wife, and the word "graciously" joins the manner, which is that the gift is to be given with a good heart and not grudgingly. "But if they waive some of it willingly" lets for the case in which the woman, of her own choice, lets part of it go. The choice has to be hers and not his, and the verse insists on the word willingly. "then you may enjoy it freely with a clear conscience" closes the verse with the permission that follows that choice, which is that the husband may use what she has given without any sense of guilt. The three phrases move from the duty, to the freedom of the giver, to the peace of the one who receives. They stand after the verse on the guardian so that the rights of women are guarded from both sides of the household, the side of the orphan's guardian and the side of the husband. The verse is short, but it makes the dower a plain duty with a plain exit, and the reader can see both at once. Nothing in the verse lets a man take from his wife what she has not freely given, and the sources read that limit as the centre of the rule.

**The dower is a right, not a favour.**

So, the verse here teaches that the dower of women is their right which must be fulfilled as a matter of obligation. Since, as a rule, all obligatory rights must be discharged cheerfully, so it should be in the case of dower, that is, 'give in good cheer'. This command is addressed to the husbands so that they themselves give their wives their dowers and not give these to others. (And give unto the women, (whom ye marry) free gift) as an obligation from Allah upon you (of their marriage portions) their dowries; (but if they of their own accord remit unto you a part thereof) if they make lawful for you to take some of the dowry, (then ye are welcome to absorb it (in your wealth) there is no blame or sin on you if you do so. And give women their dowries as a free gift; God granted free men the right to marry four women at the same time. Also addressed here are the guardians of the girls with the instruction that they should, in case they happen to receive the dower meant for the girls, give it straight to the girls and make sure that they themselves do nothing to put the money in personal use without the permission of the girls.

**The word nihlah and the cheerful gift.**

Muhammad bin Ishaq narrated from Az-Zuhri that 'Urwah said that 'A'ishah said that 'Nihlah' means 'obligatory'. Muqatil, Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj said, 'Nihlah' means 'obligatory' Ibn Jurayj added: 'specified.' Ibn Zayd said, "In Arabic, Nihlah, refers to what is necessary. This injustice was removed through the use of the word, nihlah, since nihlah in Arabic usage means 'giving something cheerfully'. And give women their dowries saduqāt plural of sudqa their bridal money mahr muhūr as a free gift nihlatan is a verbal noun a present given out of the kindness of one’s heart; but if they are pleased to offer you any of it of their own accord nafsan ‘of their own accord’ is for specification and is taken from the subject of the verb thus it refers back to ‘they’ the women meaning if their own selves are pleased that you should have something of the dowry and they give it to you then consume it with good wholesome appetite a praiseworthy consequence with no harm therein for you with regard to the Hereafter this was revealed in response to those who were opposed to this consumption. That is nearer to prevent you from Ta'ulu And give to the women (whom you marry) their Saduqat (or dowry) Nihlah (with a good heart), but if they, of their own good pleasure, remit any part of it to you, take it, and enjoy it without fear of any harm. (And give unto the women, (whom ye marry) free gift) as an obligation from Allah upon you (of their marriage portions) their dowries; (but if they of their own accord remit unto you a part thereof) if they make lawful for you to take some of the dowry, (then ye are welcome to absorb it (in your wealth) there is no blame or sin on you if you do so.

**When women give up a part of it.**

Yet if they gladly give up a part of the dowry to you, of their own free will, then there is nothing to stop you enjoying it. It means: 'if these women give up some of it out of their own sweet will, you may have it to your advantage and pleasure.'. This act of theirs hardly brought forth real forgiving of the standing right, but they, on their part, went about free of the concern for dower which, according to their thinking, was 'forgiven'. He mandated justice between [these wives] so the servant must respect what is obligatory. If he knows that he can uphold this obligation in a proper manner the choice is a permitted one.

**Before Islam, and the dowry.**

Before Islam, men used to marry without giving any dowry to their wives. Yet if they gladly give up a part of the dowry to you, of their own free will, then there is nothing to stop you enjoying it. That is nearer to prevent you from Ta'ulu And give to the women (whom you marry) their Saduqat (or dowry) Nihlah (with a good heart), but if they, of their own good pleasure, remit any part of it to you, take it, and enjoy it without fear of any harm. This verse takes up a particular right of women and aims to remove the injustice practiced in this matter. The guardians were forbidden to marry their orphan girls possessing property and beauty without being just to them, as they generally refrain from marrying them (when they are neither beautiful nor wealthy)."

5.text:
The verse gives a rule about wealth that is handed to someone who cannot manage it. "Do not entrust the incapable among your dependants with your wealth which Allah has made a means of support for you" is the first command, and it names the person who is unable to look after property, and it names what the property is for, which is to keep the household alive and in good order. The property is a provision and not a prize, and the verse puts so at its opening. "but feed and clothe them from it" turns the same wealth to the good of the dependant, so that the property is not hidden away but spent on the people it supports. The word "but" marks the turn: the guardian is not to hand over the money, and he is also not to starve the one who cannot manage it. "and speak to them kindly" closes the verse with the manner of the giving, which is gentle. The rule is not that the foolish are to be cut off from their needs, but that the money is to be handled by the one who can handle it, while the dependant is still cared for with food, clothing and good words. The verse is short and its three commands are linked, so that protecting the property and caring for the person are one work. A reader who keeps the whole verse in view will see that the guardian is never released from care, even when he is released from the duty to hand over the money. The passage before it spoke of the orphans, and this verse extends the same care to every dependant in the house, whose needs are real even when their judgment is not yet trusted.

**Who the foolish are.**

(Give not unto the foolish) do not give to those who are ignorant of the rights of women and children (your wealth which Allah hath given you to maintain) as a means of living; (but feed and clothe them from it) be yourselves responsible for feeding and clothing them, for you know better than them the right thing to do concerning sustenance and alms giving, (and speak kindly unto them) if you do not have anything to give them, promise them that you will clothe them and give to them. The foolish are those who keep you from the Real and distract you from the Lord. The foolish are those dependents and children who prefer their worldly portions over the rights of God most high. But do not O guardians give to the foolish the squanderers from among men women and children your property that is the property that is theirs but held by you which God has assigned to you as maintenance qiyāman ‘maintenance’ is the verbal noun from qāma; a variant reading has qiyaman the plural of qīma ‘value’ that is that with which property is valued meaning that the property which sustains your livelihoods and the well-being of your children lest they expend it improperly; provide for them thereof that is feed them from it and clothe them and speak to them decent words prepare for them a kind reception by giving them their property when they reach maturity. And give not unto the unwise your wealth which Allah has made a means of support for you, but feed and clothe them therewith, and speak to them words of kindness and justice And test orphans until they reach the age of marriage; if then you find sound judgment in them, release their property to them, but consume it not wastefully and hastily, fearing that they should grow up. Guardians, do not give property to those who do not know how to manage it well.

**Wealth as a means of support.**

Allah prohibited giving the unwise the freedom to do as they wish with wealth, which Allah has made as a means of support for people. It is a means of livelihood for man, supporting his existence in the world. Allah made this property a way to serve the interests of people and for them to live on it, and such people are not able to manage their wealth well. These verses affirm the role of property in man's economic effort which gives him the desire to protect it. Any misappropriation of anyone’s belongings is akin to creating a breach in God’s arrangement of bestowing a livelihood upon His servants. The last two ahadith quoted above tell us that the wealth possessed by a righteous and God-fearing person is not harmful for him because such a person, by virtue of being God-fearing, will abstain from spending it in what is sinful. As such, it is not proper on the one hand to consider its acquisition one’s goal in life, while on the other, it is extremely important that any wasteful use of property should be checked and earnest efforts be made, when it falls into the wrong hands, to restore it to its rightful owner.

**Feed and clothe them, and speak kindly.**

(but feed and clothe them therewith, and speak to them words of kindness and justice.) 'Ali bin Abi Talhah said that Ibn 'Abbas commented, "Do not give your wealth, what Allah has made you responsible for and made a means of sustenance to you, to your wife or children. But do not give to the foolish your property which God has assigned to you as maintenance; provide for them thereof and clothe them and speak to them decent words. But as for forming the intention to beg or making yourself and your dependents a burden on other people it is more appropriate to hold on to a sufficient amount from what God has assigned to you. Then you can be generous with what is in excess of your needs. (but if he is poor, let him have for himself what is just and reasonable.) Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that 'A'ishah said, "This Ayah,. (And whoever among guardians is rich, he should take no wages, but if he is poor, let him have for himself what is just and reasonable.) was revealed about the guardian of the orphan and pertains to whatever work he does for the orphan's estate.

**When the property may be handed over.**

Instead, they should be watched and tested to determine the age and time when they exhibit the ability to protect their property and the discernment of spending out of it, it is then that their property should be handed over to them. Make a firm commitment to give them their property if they get sound judgement and become able to manage it well. To remove this misunderstanding, it has been said in these verses that properties should not be handed over to the feeble-minded. In the case of an orphan, who happens to be the weakest member of society, it becomes even more imperative that his property be well-protected and he be dealt with in fairness and justice. The injunction to give orphans their property, and the women, their dower, has appeared in previous verses. It is possible that the person whose affairs are being settled is weak and cannot deal effectively with unjust treatment, but surely God will catch hold of the arbiter on the Day of Reckoning and punish him severely for any unjustified settlement. Since Allah Almighty has made you the guardian and the manager, you should, rather, hold the property in your safe custody and keep spending from it as necessary in order to feed and clothe them.

6.text:
The verse sets a test for the orphans before their property is returned to them, and it lays out the whole process in order. "Test the competence of the orphans until they reach a marriageable age" is the first step, and it puts the handing over at a time when the young person can be seen to be capable, so that the test is made in practice and not on paper. "Then if you feel they are capable of sound judgment" makes the test a matter of judgment as well as of years, and it asks the guardian to form a view. "return their wealth to them" is the duty once the test is passed, and "And do not consume it wastefully and hastily before they grow up to demand it" warns the guardian against using up what is not his, since the young person may yet be entitled to ask for it. "If the guardian is well-off" begins the rule about pay, and "they should not take compensation" means that the rich guardian takes nothing for his trouble, since the work is done out of his own means. "but if the guardian is poor" changes the case, and "let them take a reasonable provision" gives him a fair share for the work he does. The word reasonable is the measure, and the verse leaves its size to the custom of decent men. "When you give orphans back their property, call in witnesses" joins the safeguard of witnesses at the handing over, so that no one may later say the property was not returned. "And sufficient is Allah as a vigilant Reckoner" closes the verse by naming the One who counts every act. The whole passage is a careful sequence, test, return, pay and witness, and it is built so that the guardian has nothing to hide when the account is closed. Each step protects the orphan and also protects the guardian from suspicion, so that the process is open to anyone who looks at it.

**Testing the orphans before they reach maturity.**

Try test well the orphans before reaching maturity with regard the duties of religion and before they can legally manage their own affairs until they reach the age of marrying that is until they have become eligible for it through puberty or legal age which according to al-Shāfi‘ī is the completion of fifteen years; then if you perceive in them maturity that is right judgement in matters of religion and their property deliver their property to them; consume it not O guardians wastefully without due merit and in haste that is hastening to expend it fearing lest they should grow up and become mature at which time you will be obliged to hand it over to them. (and test the orphans) in this verse means exactly this. Once we know from verse 5 that minors should not be entrusted with properties until such time that their ability to discern and decide stands proved, the injunctions to educate and test such children to determine their ability follow in the next verse Verse 6: translated as 'and test the orphans until they reach marriageable age;' means that children, well before they become pubert and marriageable, should be tested through small assignments of buying and selling in order to determine their ability to conduct themselves in transactions on their own. This process of practical experimentation should continue right through upto the age of marriage-ability, that is, when they become pubert and mature. Guardians, test the orphans when they are near to reaching maturity, by giving them a part of their wealth to see how they manage it. Try well the orphans until they reach the age of marrying; then if you perceive in them maturity rushd deliver their property to them; consume it not wastefully and in haste lest they should grow up. In the case of an orphan, who happens to be the weakest member of society, it becomes even more imperative that his property be well-protected and he be dealt with in fairness and justice. (Prove orphans) test the intelligence of orphans (till they reach the marriageable age) the age of puberty; (then, if ye find them of) if you see that they possess (sound judgement) righteousness in Religion and a tendency to protect their wealth, (deliver over unto them their fortune) then give their wealth which is with you; (and devour it not squandering) it in transgression and unlawfully (and in haste) in haste lest the orphan grows older and consumes it little by little (lest they should grow up) for fear that they grow older and stop you from devouring their wealth.

**The guardian who is rich, and the guardian who is poor.**

If any man who is a guardian is rich let him be abstinent that is let him abstain from the orphan’s property and refrain from consuming it; if he is poor let him consume of it honourably that is in line with the wage for his work. And whoever among guardians is rich, he should take no wages, but if he is poor, let him have for himself what is just and reasonable (according to his work). (And whoever among guardians is rich, he should take no wages, but if he is poor, let him have for himself what is just and reasonable.) was revealed about the guardian of the orphan and pertains to whatever work he does for the orphan's estate. If any man is rich let him be abstinent; if he is poor let him consume honorably. Whoever is wealthy should not use up the property of the orphan; and whoever is poor and has no wealth should only use what is necessary. (Whoso (of the guardians) is rich) and needs not the orphan's wealth, (let him abstain generously) because of his richness from taking of the property of orphans, nor should he diminish anything from their wealth; (and whoso is poor) and needy (let him take thereof in reason (for his guardianship) in measure, such that he is not in need for the wealth of orphans; it is also said that this means: he should take from the wealth of orphans in proportion with the measure of his work regarding this wealth; and it is also said that this means: he can take from the wealth of orphans as a loan to be paid back. (but if he is poor, let him have for himself what is just and reasonable.) Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that 'A'ishah said, "This Ayah,. A lot of people fix an insignificant monthly emolument shown on paper to satisfy legal requirements but they go on spending by various other means on their person and on their family recklessly, much much beyond it.

**Calling witnesses when the property is returned.**

And when you deliver to them the orphans their property take witnesses over them that they have received it and that you are absolved of the obligation so that if any dispute occurs you are able to refer to a clear proof this is a command intended for guidance. (And when ye deliver up their fortune unto orphans) when they reach the legal age, (have (the transaction) witnessed in their presence) when you deliver it to them. If they manage it well, and show you their sound judgement, hand over their property in full. The injunction of the Qur'an is: 'then, if you perceive in them proper understanding, hand over to them their property.' Now, what is the time of this 'proper understanding' (rushd)? Allah prohibited giving the unwise the freedom to do as they wish with wealth, which Allah has made as a means of support for people.

**Maturity, and the mature guardian's judgment.**

To perceive maturity means [to perceive] decency and integrity. It is gen erosity and the preservation of honor keeping company with elders and striving to look to the good and to perform acts of devotion as decreed by the command. It is said that the one who is mature rashīd is the one who is guided to his Lord. When a need arises in him he does not rely on his own power or strength his own planning or choosing. Along with the injunction of maturity ( bulugh) in this verse, the Holy Qur'an has also answered the question as to the 'age' when a child would be taken as mature ( baligh) by saying: translated as 'until they reach marriage-ability'. This ruling sometimes applies because of being young, as young people are incapable of making wise decisions.

**Thabit, his uncle, and the orphan under his care.**

This verse was revealed about Thabit Ibn Rifa'ah al-Ansari. This was revealed about Thabit ibn Rifa'ah and his uncle. Rifa'ah died when his son Thabit was very young. The uncle of Thabit went to the Messenger of Allah, Allah bless him and give him peace, and said: The son of my brother is an orphan under my care, what is lawful for me from his wealth? And so Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

7.text:
The verse opens a new part of the surah with a rule about inheritance, and it begins with the words that give men and women an equal standing in law. "For men there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave" names the men first, and the share is in what the parents and close kin leave behind. The word share is the key, since it is a portion that belongs to the person by right and not a gift from the family. "and for women there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave" repeats the rule for the women, so that both are given a share in the same estate, and the sentence is built on the same words so that no one can read a difference into it. "whether it is little or much" makes the share a right whatever the size of the estate, and the poor estate has a share as the rich one does. "These are obligatory shares" closes the verse by calling them fixed, so that no one may decide for himself how much to give. The verse sets aside the old custom in which the women were left out, and it does so in plain words that every reader can follow. The rule opens the long passage on inheritance that comes after it, and the share it names is the base on which the other shares are built. The sources read the share as a settled thing, so the heirs are not asked to bargain over it, and the estate is divided by the rule and not by the mood of the family. The passage that follows turns from the principle to the proportions, and the sources treat each proportion as a fixed part of the one right, and the reader who has taken in the principle will find the proportions easier to hold, because each of them is a part of the same settled right. The reader is asked to hold the principle first and the sums later, since the principle is what the rest of the passage assumes. The rule is the same for every heir, whether the estate is large or small, and that sameness is the point the verse wants fixed in the mind before any of the figures appear.

**Men and women both have a share.**

(Unto the men (of a family) belongeth a share of that which parents and near kindred leave, and unto the women a share of that which parents and near kindred leave, whether it is a little or much) whether the inheritance is much or little (a legal share) a determined share whether it is much or little, but He did not specify these shares. Women are also to have a share of what they leave, which was not the way that things were in the time of ignorance before Islam, when women and children were left out of the inheritance. There is a share for men and a share for women from what is left by parents and those nearest in relation, whether the property be small or large – a legal share And when the relatives, and the orphans, and the poor are present at the time of division, give them from the property, and speak to them words of kindness and justice And let those (executors and guardians) have the same fear in their minds as they would have for their own, if they had left weak offspring behind. Allah then mentioned the share of men and women in inheritance-because they were not in the habit of giving any inheritance to women and children-saying: (There is a share for men from what is left by parents and those nearest in relation.)" We will mention this Hadith when explaining the two Ayat about inheritance.

**Pre-Islamic custom, and Umm Kuhhah.**

This is because in the pre-Islamic period women and children, even if they were male, did not inherit anything, for only older man did. This verse was revealed about Umm Kuhhah and her daughters who had an uncle who did not give them anything from their inheritance. Their father had left behind a considerable fortune which is now with Suwayd and Arfajah who have failed to give me, or my daughters, anything when they are still under my care. The following was revealed as a repudiation of pre-Islamic practices in which women and children were not given any inheritance To the men young ones and kin belongs a share a portion of what deceased parents and kinsmen leave and to the women belongs a share of what parents and kinsmen leave whether it the property be little or much. (There is a share for men from what is left by parents and those nearest in relation)." The Messenger of Allah, Allah bless him and give him peace, summoned them, and in their defence they said: Leave for now, I shall wait for what Allah relates to me concerning their matter , and they left.

**The share is fixed, whether little or much.**

This share is a right and its amount is clearly set out – as made obligatory by Allah. Allah did expound consequently on the exact value of these shares. God has made it an obligatory share apportioned to be given to them. The determining of inheritance does not vary according to virtue or good qualities nor is it different due to fault defect or sin. If a man dies leav ing two sons their rights are equivalent even if one of them is pious and God-fearing and the other wicked and disobedient. Therefore, everyone is equal in Allah's decision to inherit, even though their shares vary according to the degree of their relationship to the deceased, whether being a relative, spouse, etc. All this happened in the background when nations around the world had allowed these two weaker units of human society to remain deprived of their natural and obligatory rights.

**The share and the unlawful gain.**

But every unlawful acquisition that he makes is like filling up his belly with fire. The fact that whatever is usurped is like fire may not be apparent here, but it will become evident in the Hereafter. There is a share for men and a share for women from what is left by parents and those nearest in relation, whether the property be small or large – a legal share And when the relatives, and the orphans, and the poor are present at the time of division, give them from the property, and speak to them words of kindness and justice And let those (executors and guardians) have the same fear in their minds as they would have for their own, if they had left weak offspring behind. Man has been given freedom of action in this world, but he cannot manipulate the result of his actions. The word, 'al-aqrabun' covers all, but parents were set apart specially because of their importance. Then He said Yet some of them are those who wrong themselves and some of them are moderate and some are those who take the lead in [performing] good works by the leave of God. However, if there are relatives who are all declared to be the nearest at the same time, even if the nature of nearness in them be different, then, all of them will deserve a share in the inheritance as the father and mother alongwith children, or wife etc., for they all are the nearest, though the nature of nearness differs. He should adopt the culture of beneficence and, according to his capacity, be a giver to others. The verse declares their entitlement to their share as fixed by Islamic law and strictly forbids any attempt to decrease their due right.

8.text:
The verse is about the moment of the division, when the estate is being shared out and people who have no claim to a share are standing nearby. "If non-inheriting relatives, orphans, or the needy are present at the time of distribution" names the three people who are there, the relatives who do not inherit, the orphans, and the poor. The verse does not say they should be given a share, since they have no right to one, but it puts they should not be sent away empty. "offer them a small provision from it and speak to them kindly" tells the heirs what to do, which is to give these people something from the estate out of kindness, and to speak to them in a way that does not make them feel small. The provision is small because it is not theirs by right, and the word kindly is what makes it a gift and not a dismissal. The verse follows the rule about shares, and it reminds the heirs that the estate is not only theirs to divide, since the needy are present at the division and have a claim on the heart of the one who divides. The reader is asked to see the division as a moment of care as well as of arithmetic, and the same care runs through the next verse, which turns to the guardians and the orphans once more, so that the rules about money are read in the light of the people they serve, and to see the people who stand at the edge of it as part of the family that is being provided for.

**Relatives, orphans and the needy at the division.**

It means that distant relatives, orphans and the needy who are to be excluded from having a share in the inheritance and who, nevertheless, show up at the time of its distribution, then, it is the moral obligation of those who get a share in the inheritance that they voluntarily give them some of it, which would become an act of charity for them, and certainly, a modality of reward from Allah. And when the division is attended by kinsmen and orphans and the poor grant them out of it; and speak to them honorable words. When the division of the inheritance is attended by those who are [to be] the possessors of its shares and are the legal heirs and others [also] attend who have no [legal] portion and who are poor do not deprive them of that. There is a share for men and a share for women from what is left by parents and those nearest in relation, whether the property be small or large – a legal share And when the relatives, and the orphans, and the poor are present at the time of division, give them from the property, and speak to them words of kindness and justice And let those (executors and guardians) have the same fear in their minds as they would have for their own, if they had left weak offspring behind. In short, the fact that distant kindred, orphans and the needy assemble at the time of the distribution of inheritance should be no cause of irritation. At a time like this, when wealth and property are coming to them, without their having made any effort, simply through the mercy of Allah Almighty - then, their own hearts should beat with the urge to give whatever they can, in the way of Allah, an example of which appears in another verse (Al an'am: 6:141) cited below: And when the division of the inheritance is attended by kinsmen those of kinship who cannot inherit and orphans and the poor grant them something out of it before the division is effected; and if the inheritors are young speak to them O guardians honourable words kindly by apologising to them that it is not your possession to divide as you wish but that it is for the young inheritors.

**Who the non-inheriting relatives are.**

Some say that this stipulation was abrogated; others say that it was not only that people were all too readily neglecting it since it was encouraged but not prescribed. According to Ibn ‘Abbās however it is a duty. If relatives, orphans and the poor, who do not inherit, are present at the time the inheritance is divided, then give them, out of kindness, some of this wealth before it is divided, for they may be looking at it with desire for a share; and it came to you without you doing anything. The statement at the end of the verse : ‌ (and speak to them in fair words) gives the guideline in case these people are not satisfied with the manner and quantum of what they get but start demanding a share equal to that of everybody else, then, this demand being unjust and contrary to Shari'ah, there is no way to satisfy it, however, instead of behaving to them in a crude manner which may hurt their feelings, the actual rules-of Shari'ah should be explained to them in a polite manner. Ath-Thawri said that Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid that implementing this Ayah, "Is required from those who have anything to inherit, paid from whatever portions their hearts are satisfied with giving away. (And when kinsfolk) who are not entitled to receive a share of the inheritance (and orphans) the orphans of believers before the division of the inheritance (and the needy) the needy among believers (are present at the division) of the heritage, (bestow on them there from) give them something of the inheritance before you proceed to divide it upon those who are entitled to receive it (and speak kindly unto them) if the inheritor has not yet reached the age of puberty, by promising them to speak to the inheritor about giving them something.

**Taqwa, and the kind word.**

So, let them have Taqwa of Allah and speak truthfully Verily, those who unjustly eat up the property of orphans, they eat up only a fire into their bellies, and they will be burnt in the blazing Fire. means, let them have Taqwa of Allah when taking care of the orphan's wealth, as Ibn Jarir recorded from Al-'Awfi who reported this explanation from Ibn 'Abbas. Also, speak to them in a kind way, without any meanness. This is the meaning of His words and speak to them honorable words. When they are present at His court in the future and the Real pardons those who were obedient and gives them the rewards for their deeds He will not deprive the poor Muslims18 among you of the pardon if God wills after their having been among the family of faith ahl al-īmān.

9.text:
The verse tells the executors and guardians to think of the people in their care as their own. "Let the guardians be as concerned for the orphans as they would if they were to die and leave their own helpless children behind" is the command, and it is an instruction about concern, not only about money. The picture is the one that makes the concern real, which is the fear a parent has for children who would be left without help. "So let them be mindful of Allah and speak equitably" turns that concern into a duty before God, and it ends with the manner of speech, which is to be fair and not to deceive. The verse sits between the rules about the estate and the warning that follows, and it is the bridge between the two, so that the care for the orphan is kept in view while the wealth is being counted. It asks the guardian to feel for the orphan as for his own children, since the same fear would come to him for his own. The reader is asked to put himself in the place of the parent who is leaving children behind, and to see that the guardian who would want good for his own would want it for the orphan too. The fear of Allah is named as the thing that keeps that feeling steady, so that it does not change with the mood of the moment. The guardian who has this fear does not need a witness to be just, because he knows that the One who watches him is not absent when the door is closed, and the verse therefore asks for the inner keeping of the duty as well as its outward form.

**Concern for the orphan as for one's own children.**

Just as they would fear ruin for their own children, they ought to fear ruin for the children of any deceased person; it is also said that this means: enjoin the person who is on his deathbed that which you would enjoin yourself; and fear for the loss of his children if he were to die, as you would fear for the loss of your own children if you were to die. Let them be mindful of orphans under their guardianship, not doing any wrong to them. The third verse addresses Muslims in general exhorting them to make it certain that the inheritance of the deceased reaches his children fully and fairly. There is a share for men and a share for women from what is left by parents and those nearest in relation, whether the property be small or large – a legal share And when the relatives, and the orphans, and the poor are present at the time of division, give them from the property, and speak to them words of kindness and justice And let those (executors and guardians) have the same fear in their minds as they would have for their own, if they had left weak offspring behind. And let them fear let them be concerned for the orphans those who if they are about to leave behind them that is after their death weak offspring young children would be afraid for them; that they be ruined; let them fear God in the matter concerning orphans and let them give what they would love for their own offspring after their death; and speak to the one approached by death pertinent words the right words by enjoining him to give as voluntary almsgiving no more than the third of the inheritance and leave the remainder for the ones inheriting so that they do not end up as dependants. This is because they were in the habit of visiting people who were on their deathbeds and enjoining them to give their property to this and that person until nothing was left for their own children, so Allah prohibited them from so doing. Therefore, everyone is equal in Allah's decision to inherit, even though their shares vary according to the degree of their relationship to the deceased, whether being a relative, spouse, etc. Man has been given freedom of action in this world, but he cannot manipulate the result of his actions. And let them fear those who if they leave behind them weak offspring would be afraid for them; let them fear God and speak pertinent words.

**Fear of Allah, and fair speech.**

Allah commands whoever hears such will to fear Allah, and direct the dying man to do what is right and to be fair, being as eager to protect the inheritors of the dying man as he would be with his own. Rather He said let them fear God for He looks after the righteous. (So let them mind their duty to Allah) let them fear Allah regarding the bequeathing of more than a third of the inheritance to those who are not entitled to inheritance, (and speak) to the person who is sick [expecting to die] (justly) about his will. Also included in the general sense of the verse is that guardians of the orphaned children should protect their property and give it to them in full when they become mature. He should adopt the culture of beneficence and, according to his capacity, be a giver to others. Allah proclaims that those who unjustly consume the wealth of orphans, will be eating fire into their stomach, this is why Allah said,. The fact that whatever is usurped is like fire may not be apparent here, but it will become evident in the Hereafter.

**Concern and the fear of the guardian.**

Let whoever is present at the making of will, say what is right for the children, so that the heirs are not wronged in the will. Let those executors and guardians fear in the manner they would if they had died and left young, weak children behind them, fearing they would be ruined. So that Allah brings about others to treat well their own children after they die, as they treated the orphans well. He explained in this verse that what the Muslim should accumulate for his dependents is not wealth but fear of God taqwā and righteousness ṣalāḥ for He did not say so let them gather their wealth let them multiply real estate for them and let them leave behind household goods. They must abstain from any mode of action which may affect the share of the children adversely. They should take pains to accomplish this mission of trust and never let the least negligence on their part affect their duty; if they wish that others treat their children well after them, without causing them any harm or injustice, then, they should treat the children of others - the orphans - in the same manner. But every unlawful acquisition that he makes is like filling up his belly with fire.

10.text:
The verse names the wrong and its end. "Indeed, those who unjustly consume orphans' wealth" names the people who take what is not theirs, and the word unjustly marks the act as a wrong and not a mistake. The wrong is in the taking, and the verse does not need to describe how it is done. "wealth in fact consume nothing but fire into their bellies" is the image that follows, and it puts that what is taken is fire in the belly, even though it does not look like fire in this world. The phrase "in fact" is the verse's way of saying that the reality is other than it seems, so that a man who eats the orphan's money may see only food. "And they will be burned in a blazing Hell" closes the verse with the consequence, which is that the wrong will show itself as fire in the next life, and the blazing fire is named so that the reader can see what the price is. The verse follows the rule that the orphan's wealth must be kept whole, and it ends the passage on the guardian by naming the price of the act. The three phrases move from the act, to its hidden nature, to its public result, and the reader leaves the passage with the consequence in view. The sources treat the verse as the plainest warning in the passage, and they read the fire as the reality of what is eaten, which is why the warning is given without qualification.

**The fire in the belly, and the fire of Hell.**

This verse equates the property of the orphan with the fire of Hell. Many commentators have interpreted this metaphorically, that is, eating the property of the orphans unjustly is like stuffing one's stomach with fire - because this is what is going to happen to him ultimately in the Hereafter. According to them, whatever is eaten up from the property of the orphan unlawfully is, in reality, nothing but fire - even though, it may not look like fire at that time. Allah will place fire in their bellies on the Day of Judgement (and they will be exposed to burning flame) a blazing fire in the Hereafter. Those who take the property of orphans and spend it wrongly and unjustly, they only swallow fire into themselves: they will burn in the fire of Hell on the Day of Judgement. Surely those who eat the property of orphans wrongly will be eating only fire in their bellies and will roast in a blaze. So, let them have Taqwa of Allah and speak truthfully Verily, those who unjustly eat up the property of orphans, they eat up only a fire into their bellies, and they will be burnt in the blazing Fire.

**The unlawful gain, and what it becomes in the Hereafter.**

The fact that whatever is usurped is like fire may not be apparent here, but it will become evident in the Hereafter. The gist of the meaning of the verse is that the property of the orphan eaten up unjustly will be, in reality, the fire of Hell, though it may not be sensed as fire at that time. (Lo! Those who devour the wealth of orphans wrongfully) extortionately, (they do but swallow fire into their bellies) i.e. that which is unlawful; it is also said that this means: But every unlawful acquisition that he makes is like filling up his belly with fire. Therefore, everyone is equal in Allah's decision to inherit, even though their shares vary according to the degree of their relationship to the deceased, whether being a relative, spouse, etc.

**The wrong done to the orphan.**

One who wishes to be saved from evil consequences should not do wrong to others. So, when poor relatives, who are ineligible for inheritance, orphans, and the poor attend the division of the inheritance, which is sometimes substantial, their hearts will feel eager to have a share, seeing each eligible person assuming his share; while they are desperate, yet are not given anything. As for those wrongdoers who skewer the livers of orphans and drink the blood of the indigent, He threatens them and warns them of a fearful punishment. (To join others in worship along with Allah, magic, to kill the life which Allah has forbidden except for a just cause, to consume interest, to consume an orphan's property, to turn your back to the enemy and flee from the battlefield at the time of fighting, and to accuse chaste women who never even think of anything harmful to their chastity being good believers.) It is harsh to eat the wealth of orphans and foolishly crave their possessions. Man has been given freedom of action in this world, but he cannot manipulate the result of his actions. If one is not in a position to benefit others in any way, one should, according to Islamic standards, at least not hurt anyone’s feelings.

**The orphan's loss in the division of shares.**

So, when poor relatives, who are ineligible for inheritance, orphans, and the poor attend the division of the inheritance, which is sometimes substantial, their hearts will feel eager to have a share, seeing each eligible person assuming his share; while they are desperate, yet are not given anything. It not only amounts to wasting of property but also means causing loss to orphans and absent inheritors whose due rights are attached to the total property. It is quite possible that they are left with no option but give their permission lest they are disgraced before others. He should adopt the culture of beneficence and, according to his capacity, be a giver to others. He acts as the deputy of the helpless and disputes with the wrongdoers for their sake. Common generalizations of the Holy Qur'an also support the view that whatever deeds, good or evil, man is doing, these very deeds are the trees, the flowers and the fruits of Paradise, or the embers of Hell - even though, their form here is different, but these will come forth on the Day of Doom transformed in their true forms. Ath-Thawri said that Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid that implementing this Ayah, "Is required from those who have anything to inherit, paid from whatever portions their hearts are satisfied with giving away.
